title: Reading a finance paper
objectives: Read a paper’s abstract, data section and main table in that order.

screens.title: Two abstracts
screens.prose: Two abstracts, broken into claims. The first is Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers". We call it JT. The second is a made-up note on a technical rule.

rows: Buying past 3 to 12 month winners and selling losers earns positive returns over the next 3 to 12 months.
The 6-month/6-month strategy earns a compounded excess return of 12.01% a year.
Part of the first-year gain reverses in the second and third years.
The rule's Sharpe ratio is 3.1 on daily FTSE 100 data from 2015 to 2020.
The rule adapts to changing market regimes.

screens.question: Tap every claim you could check with data and a number.

hints.text: For each claim, ask: what would I compute, and on which data?
The Sharpe claim names a market, a period and a number.
Four claims name something you could compute. Two name nothing you could measure.

feedback.correct: Correct. Four claims name a number you could compute.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep the claims that say what to compute and on which data.

byKey.jt-only: You left out the Sharpe claim. It names a market, a period and a number, so you can test it.
byKey.r4: "Adapts to regimes" names no number and no test. What would you compute to refute it?
byKey.r5: Who trusts a rule is not a measurement of the rule. Leave that one out.
byKey.r0: You missed the first JT claim. Positive returns over 3 to 12 months is a sign you can compute.
byKey.r1: You missed the 12.01% claim. It names a strategy and a number.
byKey.r2: You missed the reversal claim. Returns in years two and three can be measured.

explain.text: You kept the three JT claims and the Sharpe claim. Testable is not believable: the backtest course called any Sharpe above 2 a warning sign. The last two claims cannot be wrong, so they tell you nothing.

screens.title: The reading order
screens.prose: A practitioner reads a paper to decide, fast, whether its claim is worth testing. Each section answers one question. The order you read them in decides how soon you can say no.

rows: Why the authors think the result matters
The claim and its headline number
Which shares, which dates, which source
Whether the result survives other choices

screens.question: Tap the five sections in the order you would read them.

hints.text: Which section states the claim you are testing?
Start with the abstract. Then ask what the claim rests on.
Abstract, then data, then the main table, then robustness. The introduction comes last.

feedback.correct: Correct. Claim, data, numbers, robustness, then the story.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the claim first, then what it rests on: the data, then the numbers.

byKey.intro-first: You started with the introduction. It is the authors' case for the paper, so read it once you know what the numbers say.
byKey.order: You have every section, in a different order. Each one should answer a question the last one raised.

explain.text: The abstract gives the claim. The data section and the main table tell you whether you could reproduce it, and robustness whether it is fragile. The introduction sells the result, so read it last, when you can judge the sale.

screens.title: What the strategy costs
screens.prose: JT's strategy buys the winner decile and sells short the loser decile, in equal amounts. A short sale raises cash: you borrow the shares and sell them.
screens.question: Before margin and fees, how much of your own capital does the position need?

options.text: £0: the short sale pays for the purchase

options.why: You counted the purchase but not the £1,000,000 the short sale raises.
You added the two legs. That is the gross exposure, not the capital the trades need.

options.text: −£1,000,000: you are paid to hold it
options.why: You counted the short sale's cash but not the purchase it funds.

hints.text: Add up the Cash column.
The two cash amounts have opposite signs.

feedback.correct: Correct. The trades fund each other: a **zero-cost** portfolio.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the cash each leg uses and the cash each leg raises.

explain.text: The short sale raises the £1,000,000 that buys the winners, so the net cash is £0. JT call this a zero-cost portfolio, and its return is a spread per £1 long and £1 short. A broker still asks for margin, which the paper's returns leave out.

screens.title: Extract the design
screens.prose: Before any data, write down what the abstract commits the paper to: the universe, the period and the headline number.

rows: Shares that did well over the past 3 to 12 months keep doing well over the next 3 to 12 months. Past losers keep doing badly.
The sample is NYSE and AMEX shares from 1965 to 1989.
Buying winners and selling losers on 6-month returns, held 6 months, earns a compounded excess return of 12.01% a year.

state.caption: Our paraphrase. Figures as the paper reports them.

screens.question: Fill in the four cells from the abstract.

hints.text: Each cell is in one of the three sentences.
The second sentence holds the universe and the period.
1965, 1989, NYSE and AMEX, and 12.01.

feedback.correct: Correct. That is the paper's universe, period and headline.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Copy each item from the abstract as written.

explain.text: The second sentence fixes the universe and the dates, and the third the headline. These four facts are your replication's first targets. Write them down before you see any data of your own.

screens.title: The signal
screens.prose: The universe and dates say where to look. The signal says what to rank on.

rows: Shares that did well over the past 3 to 12 months keep doing well over the next 3 to 12 months. Past losers keep doing badly.
The sample is NYSE and AMEX shares from 1965 to 1989.
Buying winners and selling losers on 6-month returns, held 6 months, earns a compounded excess return of 12.01% a year.

state.caption: Our paraphrase. Figures as the paper reports them.

screens.question: What does JT rank shares on?

options.text: Each share's return over the past 3 to 12 months
Each share's return over the next 3 to 12 months
options.why: That is the holding period. It is not known when the ranking is made.
Ranking on size is a different study. JT rank on past returns.

options.text: Each share's return in the last month alone
options.why: One month is shorter than any JT window. Their windows run 3 to 12 months.

hints.text: What is known at the moment the shares are ranked?
The first sentence names two windows: past and next.
The past window is the signal. The next window is when you hold.

feedback.correct: Correct. The signal is the past 3 to 12 month return.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The signal must be known when you rank.

explain.text: JT rank on the past 3 to 12 month return, then hold for the next 3 to 12 months. The past window is the formation period and the next one the holding period. Lesson 2 names them J and K.

screens.title: Raw or adjusted
screens.prose: Not every paper quotes the same number in its abstract and its main table. Your own replication of Paper Q gives a raw spread of 0.85% a month.

rows: A risk-adjusted alpha of 0.6% a month
A raw winners-minus-losers spread of 0.9% a month, t 2.8

state.caption: Paper Q is made up for this screen.

screens.question: Which reported number do you compare your 0.85% with?

options.text: Table 2's raw 0.9%: it measures the same thing as yours

options.why: You compared a raw spread with a risk-adjusted one. They measure different things.
Averaging two different measures gives a number nobody computed.
Both can be right. An alpha subtracts what a risk model predicts from the raw return.

hints.text: Is your 0.85% raw or risk-adjusted?
Table 2 reports a raw spread.
Compare like with like: raw with raw.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the reported number that is measured the way yours is.

explain.text: Your 0.85% is raw, so its partner is Table 2's raw 0.9%. The 0.6% alpha needs a risk model you have not run yet. Note both numbers, and which one each of your results answers.

screens.title: Return on what
screens.prose: A colleague has read the same abstract and written a one-line note.

rows: "JT report 12.01% a year for 6/6. So £100,000 in the strategy makes £12,010 a year."

screens.question: What is wrong with the note?

options.text: 12.01% is a spread on a zero-cost position: per £1 long and £1 short, before costs

options.why: You read a long-short spread as a return on capital. The position needs no capital, so the spread is not a return on £100,000.
12.01% is already a yearly figure. It compounds from about 0.95% a month.
The paper reports winners minus losers, not the winners alone.

hints.text: How much capital did the position on the last screens need?
A zero-cost position has no capital to earn a return on.
The 12.01% is earned per £1 long and £1 short. Costs and margin are extra.

feedback.correct: Correct. The 12.01% is a spread, not a return on capital.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the 12.01% is a percentage of.

byKey.capital: You read a long-short spread as a return on capital. The position needs no capital, so the spread is not a return on £100,000.

explain.text: The strategy earns 12.01% a year on each £1 long, financed by £1 short. What £100,000 earns depends on how much gross exposure it supports, and on margin and costs. The paper reports none of that, so the note's £12,010 is not in the paper.

screens.title: The headline number
screens.prose: A momentum paper's headline is a spread, earned with no capital of its own. $$r_{\text{WML}} = \bar r_{W} - \bar r_{L}$$ Here $\bar r_{W}$ is the winners' average return and $\bar r_{L}$ the losers'. Reading the paper means finding, for that one number, its universe, period, signal, holding rule and table.
screens.question: Winners return 1.8% and losers 0.9% in a month. What is $r_{\text{WML}}$?

options.why: You added the legs. The losers are sold, so their return is subtracted.
That is the winners alone. The spread subtracts the losers.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the losers' return from the winners'.

explain.text: You subtracted the losers' 0.9% from the winners' 1.8%. That spread is what a long-short paper reports. It is a return per £1 on each side, not on capital.

screens.title: The first hour
screens.prose: You find a new momentum paper on SSRN. The roadmap's other two sources are arXiv q-fin and WorldQuant BRAIN. You have one hour before deciding whether to replicate it.

rows: Raw or adjusted? Gross or net?

state.caption: A template for the first page of your notes.

screens.question: Which notes belong in the margin after that hour? Select all that apply.

options.text: The universe and dates the data section states
The exact signal: window, skip and weighting
Which table and cell the headline comes from
Whether returns are raw or adjusted, and gross or net of costs

options.why: Where the authors work does not change what you must compute.

options.text: How often the paper is cited
options.why: Citations say the paper is known, not that its table replicates.

hints.text: What would you need to compute the headline yourself?
Each template line is one thing you need.
Universe, signal, the source cell and the measure: four notes. The other two do not change the computation.

feedback.correct: Correct. Four notes, each one something you must compute or match.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep only what you need to reproduce the headline.

explain.text: Each note you kept is an input to the computation or a definition of the target. Institutions and citations change neither. With these four notes you can decide in an hour whether the replication is feasible.

ideas: Read the abstract, the data, the main table and robustness, and the introduction last.
A testable claim names a universe, a period, a signal, a holding rule and a number.
JT's 12.01% a year is a spread on a zero-cost position, not a return on capital.

formula.name: Winners minus losers
formula.note: Per £1 long and £1 short, before costs.

summary.trap: Applying 12.01% to your capital: the position needs none, so the spread is not a return on it.

quiz.prose: You have the abstract of a new paper open.
quiz.question: Which section do you read next?

options.why: The introduction argues the result matters. Check what it rests on first.
The conclusion repeats the claim. You need what it rests on.
References show where ideas came from, not what this paper computed.

feedback.correct: Correct. After the claim, the data it rests on.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Next comes what the claim rests on.

explain.text: The abstract gives the claim, and the data section tells you whether you could reproduce it. The main table and robustness follow. The introduction comes last.

quiz.prose: You buy £2,000,000 of winners with the proceeds of selling £2,000,000 of losers short. Over a month the winners return 3% and the losers 1%.
quiz.question: What is the month's profit in £, before costs?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The long leg gains, and the short leg loses what the losers gain.

byKey.sum: You added the losers' gain. You are short them, so their 1% rise costs you £20,000.
byKey.long: You counted the winners only. The short losers rose 1%, which costs £20,000.

explain.text: The winners make 3% of £2,000,000, which is £60,000. The losers rise 1%, which costs the short side £20,000. The spread of 2% on £2,000,000 gives the same £40,000.

quiz.prose: A paper's abstract quotes an alpha of 0.5% a month. Its main table shows a raw spread of 0.8% a month. Your raw spread is 0.7%.
quiz.question: Which comparison is the right one?

options.why: You compared a raw spread with an alpha. They measure different things.

options.text: 0.7% against 0.65%, the average of the two
options.why: An average of two different measures is not a target anyone computed.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Match your measure to the paper's.

explain.text: Your number is raw, so it answers the table's raw 0.8%. The alpha needs the paper's risk model. Compare it only once you have run that model too.

quiz.prose: An abstract claims a strategy "earns 12% a year" on a zero-cost position.
quiz.question: A book holds £500,000 long and £500,000 short. What does it earn in a year at that spread, before costs?

feedback.correct: Correct. 12% of the £500,000 on each side.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The spread is earned per £1 long and £1 short.

byKey.gross: You applied 12% to the £1,000,000 gross. The spread is per £1 long and £1 short, so apply it to £500,000.
byKey.capital: The position needs no capital, but it still earns the spread on each £1 long.

explain.text: The spread is earned per £1 long and £1 short, so £500,000 a side earns 12% of £500,000. That is £60,000 a year before costs. The capital you put up does not enter the sum.
